name: American Stout
title: American Stout: Style Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: American stout explained: a roasty, hop forward stout with more bite than its Irish cousin, and what to eat with it in India.
tagline: A stout with an American accent: more roast, more hops, more alcohol than the Irish version.
tastes:
Take a dry Irish stout, raise the strength to around 6 or 7 percent, push the roast, and then hop it like an American pale ale. That is close to an American stout. It shows up in the US craft boom of the 1980s and 1990s as brewers applied their love of Cascade and Centennial to darker beers.

The roast is the backbone: coffee, dark chocolate and a slightly burnt edge. Against it, citrus and pine hops give a bright, resinous lift that you would never find in a pint of Irish stout. Bitterness is firm, often in the 40s or 50s on the IBU scale, and the finish is drier than you expect for a beer this dark.

The best ones keep the two halves in balance. Too much hop and it tastes like a black IPA; too little and it is just a strong porter.

profile.look: Black and opaque, or very dark brown with ruby edges against the light. Generous, long lasting tan head.
profile.aroma_flavour: Roasted coffee, cocoa and a faint burnt note, with citrus, pine or resin from American hops. Some caramel sweetness, but roast leads.
profile.mouthfeel: Medium to full body, smooth, with moderate carbonation. Firm bitterness and a fairly dry, roasty finish.
profile.ingredients: Pale malt with roasted barley, black and chocolate malts and some crystal. American hops such as Cascade, Centennial or Chinook, sometimes dry hopped. Clean American ale yeast.

in_india: American stout is a good gateway for Indian IPA drinkers who think dark beer means sweet beer. The hop character fades in a warm supply chain faster than the roast does, so it is at its best on tap at a brewpub that brewed it. At around 6 to 7 percent it is too heavy for a summer lunch, but right for monsoon evenings and winter in the north, with grilled or fried food.

pairings.why: The roast and resin hops cut through the ghee and match the toasted red chilli.
Char and black pepper meet the roast, and the hop bitterness keeps a rich vegetarian kebab from feeling heavy.
Vinegar, garlic and chilli need a beer with backbone; the roast and hops stand up to all three.

pairings.food: Chocolate brownie with vanilla ice cream
pairings.why: Cocoa echoes the roast, and the beer's bitterness keeps the sweetness in check.
